lesson.title: Adjectives & the Silent -s
lesson.subtitle: Feminine -e wakes the sleeping final consonant (grand → grande), plural -s stays silent, and colors follow the noun

hook.title: Why the Masculine Form Sounds Shorter Than the Feminine
hook.content: Listen to grand ('big/tall'): in the masculine, the final d is completely silent (/ɡʁɑ̃/). Now add the feminine -e for a feminine noun like la maison: grande (/ɡʁɑ̃d/). That silent -e acts like a shield that protects the d from disappearing, waking the consonant back up! The exact same thing happens across French adjectives: petit (/pəti/) → petite (/pətit/), vert (/vɛʁ/) → verte (/vɛʁt/), content (/kɔ̃tɑ̃/) → contente (/kɔ̃tɑ̃t/).

footnotes.title: Why English borrowed 'petite' with the T pronounced
footnotes.content: English borrowed the feminine form petite for clothing sizes, which is why English speakers pronounce the final T — whereas French masculine petit drops the T completely!

pattern.title: Paint the Object First, Then Color It
pattern.content: In English you say 'the green garden' or 'a black coffee' — adjective before noun. In French, descriptive adjectives (especially colors, shapes, and nationalities) come AFTER the noun: le jardin vert ('the garden green'), un café noir ('a coffee black'), la maison blanche ('the house white'). First you name what the thing is; then you paint it. And in the plural, French writes an -s on both noun and adjective (les jardins verts), but that plural -s is completely silent!
pattern.linguist_note: Post-nominal adjective placement is the Romance default; only a small high-frequency set of short evaluative adjectives (BAGS, Sprig 1103) precedes the noun.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: putting color adjectives before the noun English-style (*le vert jardin). Name the noun first, then paint it: le jardin vert!

exercises.prompt: Match each masculine adjective (silent final consonant) with its feminine form (awakened consonant):
exercises.meaning: grand /ɡʁɑ̃/ (big, m.), petit /pəti/ (small, m.), vert /vɛʁ/ (green, m.), blanc /blɑ̃/ (white, m.), bon /bɔ̃/ (good, m.)
exercises.explanation: Adding feminine -e wakes up the final d, t, or n (and turns blanc into blanche).

exercises.prompt: What is the word-for-word French order of 'Le jardin vert'?
exercises.explanation: French names the object first (le jardin) and paints its color second (vert).
la maison takes feminine blanche right after the noun, and feminine grande after est.

exercises.idea: I want a black coffee please
cues: I want a coffee black → Je veux un café noir
idea_parts: want + noun + color → Je veux un café noir
exercises.target_answer: Je veux un café noir, s'il vous plaît
exercises.meaning: I want a black coffee, please
exercises.explanation: noir follows café because color adjectives sit after the noun.

diagnosis.cue: Place color adjectives after the noun: un café noir.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Le jardin est vert et la maison est blanche
exercises.target_answer: Le jardin est vert et la maison est blanche
exercises.meaning: The garden is green and the house is white
cues: masculine clause: Le jardin est vert
feminine clause: et la maison est blanche
exercises.explanation: vert has a silent t; blanche wakes up as /ʃ/.
exercises.affirmation: You contrasted masculine vert and feminine blanche cleanly.

summary.outcome: Agree adjectives in gender and number, hear the consonant awakened by feminine -e, and place colors after the noun.

use_example.german: Un café noir à la table rouge.
use_example.english: A black coffee at the red table.

summary.takeaway: Feminine -e wakes the sleeping final consonant, and colors always paint the noun from behind.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1101] The e and the s): see how Adjectives & the Silent -s leads directly into The e and the s.

twist.explanation: rouge already ends in -e in both genders; petite adds -e to agree with la table.

foreshadow.line: Having mastered Adjectives & the Silent -s, look ahead to Topic 12 (The Near Future), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 10 (avoir & the H It Lost) now pays off directly inside Adjectives & the Silent -s: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

grand.etymology_derivation: English 'grand' came straight from French; the feminine adds a silent -e, which wakes the silent d into sound: grand /ɡʁɑ̃/ → grande /ɡʁɑ̃d/.

petit.etymology_derivation: English 'petite' is the French feminine form, borrowed whole — the masculine is petit.

bon.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus 'good' — English borrowed the word back as 'bonus', a good thing added.

vert.etymology_derivation: Latin viridis → verdant, verdure — the green English kept in poetry.

blanc.etymology_derivation: Germanic blank 'shining white' → French blanc, English blank and blanket (the white cloth).

bleu.shift_rule: Frankish blao — one Germanic word, two languages
bleu.etymology_derivation: Frankish *blao gave English blue and French bleu — a Germanic word inside Romance, no shift needed.

rouge.etymology_derivation: Latin rubeus 'red' — the same stone English calls ruby. Rouge crossed into English as the makeup word.

noir.etymology_derivation: Placed after the noun, like all color adjectives.

jardin.etymology_derivation: Frankish *gardo gave English garden/yard and French jardin.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
